question.:question/problem:
Find the general solution to $\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{\mathrm{d}t}=-2s^2.$ For $s\ne 0$.

$s=($ {{field-1}} $+K)^{-1}$, where $K$ is an arbitrary real constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we separate variables and integrate both sides with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s^2}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{\mathrm{d}t} & =-2 \\ \int \frac{1}{s^2}\,\mathrm{d}s & =\int -2\,\mathrm{d}t \\ -\frac{1}{s} & =- 2 t+C\end{aligned}
$$

This is a general solution in implicit form. Solving for $s$ gives

$$
s=\frac{1}{2 t+K}=(2 t+K)^{-1}
$$

where $K=-C$. Work on intervals where the denominator is nonzero.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general solution to $\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t}=-0.02(T-15)$ for $T\ne 15.$

$T=15+K\cdot$ {{field-1}}, where $K$ is an arbitrary nonzero constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we separate variables and integrate both sides with respect to $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t} & =-0.02(T-15) \\ \frac{1}{T-15}\cdot \frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t} & =-0.02 \\ \int \frac{1}{T-15}\cdot \frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int -0.02\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{\text{d}T}{T-15} & =-0.02\int \,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-15| & =-0.02t+C\end{aligned}
$$

This is a perfectly valid general solution. However, if we want to write $T=T(t)$ explicitly, then we can solve for $T.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|T-15| & =-0.02t+C \\ |T-15| & ={e}^{-0.02t+C} \\ |T-15| & =K\,{e}^{-0.02t}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary positive constant.

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be both positive and negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =15+K\,{e}^{-0.02t}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-3)$ for $y\ne 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-3) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-3) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x-3)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x-3)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x-3)\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-3)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-3)+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-3)+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-3)+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-3)}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-3)},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-3)}.
$$

Here $K$ is arbitrary and nonzero.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x-3)}$ for $y\ne 0$ and $-\frac{\pi }{2}<(x-3)<\frac{\pi }{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x-3)} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x-3)} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x-3)} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={sec}^{2}⁡(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(x-3)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(x-3)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(x-3)\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-3)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-3)+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-3)+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-3)+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-3)}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-3)},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-3)}.
$$

Here $K$ is arbitrary and nonzero.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}={(x-3)}^{2}y$ for $y\ne 0.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {(x-3)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {(x-3)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {(x-3)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\frac{1}{3}\,{(x-3)}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\frac{1}{3}\,{(x-3)}^{3}+C.

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{{(x-3)}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{(x-3)}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{(x-3)}^{3}/3}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{{(x-3)}^{3}/3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
